title: A Simple and Efficient Option for Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment: Pneumatic Retinopexy
condition_or_topic: Pneumatic retinopexy (PR) for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD)
clinical_background: PR has been used to treat RRD for over 30 years. It is a relatively inexpensive procedure that can be performed quickly under topical anesthesia, including in an office setting, and causes less tissue trauma than scleral buckling (SB) or pars plana vitrectomy (PPV). Prior reports describe its effectiveness for detachments in the upper 8 clock hours (upper 2/3) when breaks meet specified size and proximity criteria and the ocular media permit visualization and laser treatment. Grade C and D proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) has been strongly linked to procedural failure. If PR fails, SB or PPV remains possible; prior literature has proposed that PR failure does not affect final visual acuity.
objectives: To report the anatomical and functional outcomes of PR for RRD.
study_design: Retrospective review of medical records from patients who underwent pneumatic retinopexy (PR) for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) between December 2013 and May 2017.

population.description: Patients with primary RRD selected for PR; 21 eyes from 21 patients were included in the analysis.
inclusion_criteria: Primary retinal detachment involving the upper 2/3 of the retina (from 8 to 4 clock quadrants), with a single break no wider than 1 clock hour or multiple closely located breaks.
exclusion_criteria: Aphakia or pseudophakia with an anterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL).
Age younger than 18 years, anticipated inability to maintain head positioning, or possible flight in the following 6 weeks; PR was avoided in these circumstances.
population.care_setting: Procedures were performed in an operating room at a tertiary referral center.

interventions: PR under topical anesthesia, with paracentesis followed by intravitreal injection of 0.3 ml pure C3F8gas; patients were instructed to position their heads so the gas bubble compressed the retinal break.
Indirect laser photocoagulation around the break within the following 72 hours when the adjacent retina was attached.
In cases receiving 360-degree laser retinopexy, laser was applied to attached retina between the ora serrata and the equator before PR, then completed after the procedure.
Topical antibiotics for 10 days and steroids tapered at the end of the first month.
PPV was the treatment selected when PR failed. Cryotherapy was not used.
comparators: Successful versus failed PR cases were compared on clinical and demographic factors.
Outcomes were compared according to whether 360-degree laser retinopexy was applied.

primary: Primary anatomical success, defined as an attached retina at the end of 2 months without an additional surgical procedure.
secondary: Failure to flatten the retina by the fifth postoperative day sufficiently for laser retinopexy, failure to achieve reattachment, or re-detachment as the gas bubble shrank.
Functional outcome assessed through visual acuity.
Complications and adverse events attributable to PR.
Associations of demographic and clinical characteristics with anatomical outcome.

statistical_methods: Descriptive analyses summarized demographic characteristics, presentation findings, and anatomical and functional outcomes. Categorical data were reported as counts and percentages, and continuous data as medians (interquartile range). Skewed data were compared with the Mann Whitney U test; categorical variables were assessed with Chi square or Fisher’s exact tests. Analyses used SPSS software (version 23.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA), with p <0.05 considered statistically significant.
follow_up: Examinations were scheduled for the first day, first week, and first and second months after PR, with subsequent follow-up determined by clinical status. Patients followed for less than 2 months were excluded. The reported median follow-up was 10 months (4-38).
interpretation: In selected cases of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, PR produced anatomical success in 13 (61.9%) eyes and was not associated with an observed attributable adverse event. In this series, 360-degree laser retinopexy was the only factor significantly associated with success; age, gender, visual acuity, lens status, macular involvement, detachment extent and number of breaks were not. The authors suggest that the laser barrier may help prevent new or overlooked breaks from causing failure, although 3 cases developed re-detachment despite laser retinopexy. A further eye detached 9 months after initially successful PR because of a new break beside the earlier laser sites; the authors question whether this late event should count as a failure of the initial procedure.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors consider their 61.9% success rate consistent with published PR rates of 44% to 94%, averaging 74.4%. They cite a review of 422 cases reporting 60.7% success with PR alone and a study by Cohen and co-workers reporting 59.5% primary success. They note that published success rates are higher for PPV (71-96.7%) and SB (68.2–93.7%), while describing PR as quicker, less expensive and associated with fewer complications. Rootman and co-workers identified large tears, pseudophakia and PVR as major factors associated with PR failure; the present study found no significant association with lens status, although its small sample may have influenced that result. Previous studies reported that new breaks were most often in lower or previously unaffected quadrants. Mudvari et al reported that re-detachment occurred mainly during the first 4 weeks after PR, while another cited report indicates that it can occur during the first year. The authors also describe conflicting prior findings on whether lattice degeneration affects PR outcomes.
clinical_implications: PR remains an option for selected cases of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, with a reasonable prospect of success and limited discomfort or observed complications in this series.
Laser retinopexy may seal a break after retinal attachment, while 360-degree treatment may protect against failure from new or missed breaks; neither eliminated re-detachment in every treated case.
The absence of a significant association between lens status and success in this series should be interpreted cautiously because of the small sample.
Re-detachment can occur later in the first year, even after an initially successful procedure.
practice_implications: Assess the number and location of retinal breaks carefully before PR.
The authors avoided PR in eyes with grade C or worse PVR because the procedure may not overcome the associated traction and retinal shortening.
Consider the possibility of late re-detachment after PR.
limitations: The study was retrospective and had a small sample.
As a tertiary referral center, the clinic commonly sees complex rhegmatogenous retinal detachment with substantial PVR, which may have biased treatment selection.
The duration of detachment was not considered, although the authors expect longer symptom duration to be associated with worse outcomes.
Lattice degeneration was not considered when selecting the surgical approach.
The study did not investigate the new breaks responsible for failure or evaluate PPV outcomes after failed PR.
open_questions: Whether lattice degeneration affects PR outcomes remains disputed in the cited literature.
The authors could not rule out an effect of lens status on success because of their small sample.
future_directions: The authors identify outcomes of PPV after failed PR as a subject for a separate study.

main_findings.description: PR achieved retinal reattachment and was classified as successful.
main_findings.context: The study included 21 eyes of 21 patients. Primary success required an attached retina at the end of 2 months without additional surgery. The reported median follow-up was 10 months (4-38).

main_findings.description: PR did not achieve the intended anatomical outcome in these cases.
Use of 360-degree laser retinopexy was significantly associated with anatomical success.
main_findings.context: Among patients receiving 360-degree laser retinopexy, 13 were successful and 5 failed; among those not receiving it, 0 were successful and 3 failed.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: No adverse events attributed to PR were observed in the 21 included eyes.
notable_adverse_events: Increased IOP: no event attributed to PR was observed.
Endophthalmitis: no event attributed to PR was observed.
Subsequent PVR: no case was observed among the successful cases.
ERM: no case was observed among the successful cases.

subgroup_analyses: Age was not significantly associated with outcome: median (interquartile range) was 59 (10) in failed cases and 56 (16) in successful cases; p=0.374.
Detachment extent in clock hours was not significantly associated with outcome: median (interquartile range) was 4 (1) in failed cases and 3 (2) in successful cases; p=0.275.

Best corrected visual acuity at presentation in logMAR was not significantly associated with outcome: median (interquartile range) was 0.2 (0.18) in failed cases and 0.3 (0.3) in successful cases; p=0.121.
Gender was not significantly associated with outcome (p=0.174). Failed cases comprised 7 males (87.5%) and 1 female (12.5%); successful cases comprised 7 males (53.8%) and 6 females (46.2%).

Lens status was not significantly associated with outcome (p=1.000). Failed cases included 5 phakic eyes (62.5%) and 3 pseudophakic eyes (37.5%); successful cases included 8 phakic eyes (61.5%) and 5 pseudophakic eyes (38.5%).

Macular status was not significantly associated with outcome (p=0.325). In failed cases, the macula was off in 3 eyes (37.5%) and on in 5 (62.5%); in successful cases, it was off in 2 eyes (15.4%) and on in 11 (84.6%).

The number of breaks was not significantly associated with outcome (p=0.381). Among failed cases, 7 eyes (87.5%) had 1 break and 1 eye (12.5%) had 2; among successful cases, 13 eyes (100.0%) had 1 break and 0 (0.0%) had 2.

360-degree laser retinopexy was significantly associated with success (p=0.042). Among failed cases, 5 (62.5%) received it and 3 (37.5%) did not; among successful cases, 13 (100.0%) received it and 0 (0.0%) did not.

main_conclusion: The authors consider pneumatic retinopexy an effective surgical option for selected cases of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, with a reasonable rate of anatomical success and limited discomfort or complications.
narrative_summary:
This retrospective study evaluated anatomical and functional outcomes after pneumatic retinopexy for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. The analysis included 21 eyes of 21 patients treated with C3F8; cases with follow-up shorter than 2 months were excluded. Eligibility focused on primary detachments involving the upper 2/3 of the retina, with a single break no wider than 1 clock hour or closely situated multiple breaks. Patients were examined after treatment, and retinal attachment at 2 months without additional surgery defined primary success.

Pneumatic retinopexy failed in 8 cases (38.1%), which underwent pars plana vitrectomy; additional breaks were identified in 4 of these cases. After a median follow-up of 10 months (4-38), 13 (61.9%) eyes remained attached and pneumatic retinopexy was considered successful. One initially successful case developed a new detachment 9 months after treatment because of a fresh break adjacent to earlier laser treatment. The authors observed no adverse events attributable to pneumatic retinopexy, including increased intraocular pressure or endophthalmitis. In their comparisons, 360-degree laser retinopexy was the sole factor significantly associated with anatomical success (p = 0.042). They identify the retrospective design, small sample, potential treatment-selection bias at their tertiary referral center, and lack of consideration of detachment duration as limitations.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: The study assessed the results of pneumatic retinopexy (PR) for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). Investigators retrospectively examined visual acuity, lens status, detachment location, break count, follow-up duration and demographic characteristics. Every case received C3F8 gas; patients whose PR failed underwent pars plana vitrectomy. Follow-up shorter than 2 months was an exclusion criterion. The analysis included 21 eyes from 21 patients: 14 males and 7 females, with a median age of 59 (18-68). Eight cases were pseudophakic and 13 were phakic. Preoperative visual acuity ranged from hand motions to 1.0. Median detachment extent was 4 (2-7) clock hours. A single break was identified before surgery in 19 cases, and 18 cases received peripheral retinal laser photocoagulation covering 360 degrees. This laser treatment was significantly associated with success. Retinal reattachment occurred in 13 (61.9%) cases, and no complication attributable to PR was observed. The authors consider PR safe and effective for appropriately selected cases.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: PR has been used to treat RRD for over 30 years. It is rapid, straightforward and inexpensive, can be performed under topical anesthesia in an office, and causes less tissue trauma than scleral buckling (SB) or pars plana vitrectomy (PPV). Prior evidence describes effectiveness for RRD in the upper 8 clock hours of the retina (upper 2/3), with either one break no wider than 1 clock hour or multiple breaks neither farther apart nor larger than 1 clock hour. The ocular media must permit visualization of every break and indirect laser retinopexy. Grade C and D proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) has been strongly linked to procedural failure. Earlier reports describe minor adverse effects and indicate that PR avoids major complications associated with SB, including extra-ocular muscle imbalance, diplopia and persistent discomfort, and with PPV, including cataract. If PR fails, SB or PPV remains possible; prior authors have also proposed that failed PR does not affect final visual acuity (VA). This study aimed to describe anatomic and functional outcomes of PR in RRD.

document_sections.heading: MATERIALS AND METHODS
document_sections.content: This retrospective study reviewed records of patients treated with PR from December 2013 to May 2017 and was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki. Recorded variables were demographics, initial VA, lens status, tear location and width, detachment location and extent in clock hours, number of tears, presence and grade of PVR, and follow-up duration.

document_sections.heading: Participants
document_sections.content: PR was used for primary retinal detachment involving the upper 2/3 (from 8 to 4 clock quadrants), with either a single break of maximal width 1 clock hour or closely situated multiple breaks. Exclusions were opaque media, aphakia, pseudophakia with an anterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL), PVR grade C or worse, and intraocular pressure (IOP) greater than 22 mmHg. PR was avoided in patients younger than 18 years, those unlikely to maintain head positioning, and those who might fly within the following 6 weeks. Patients followed for less than 2 months were excluded from analysis.

document_sections.heading: Injection Procedure
document_sections.content: Procedures took place in an operating room under topical anesthesia and sterile conditions. After eyelid draping, povidone iodine 5% was placed on the ocular surface and a speculum held the lids apart. A horizontal-quadrant paracentesis preceded injection of 0.3 ml pure C3F8 gas, prepared in a tuberculin syringe through a Millipore filter. A 30-gauge needle entered 3.5 mm behind the limbus in the quadrant opposite the retinal break and was directed toward the globe's center to avoid the lens. Gas was delivered slowly and continuously while the entry site remained uppermost; keeping the needle tip within the forming bubble helped produce one bubble, following the technique described by Hilton and Grizzard. A cotton-tip applicator compressed the entry site during needle withdrawal, after which the globe was turned to move the bubble away from that site. Central retinal artery pulsation was checked immediately by indirect ophthalmoscopy. If IOP was very high or pulsation was absent, pressure at the scleral edge of the paracentesis was used to lower IOP through it. Patients were instructed to sit with the head upright and tilted so the bubble pressed against the break. Topical antibiotics were prescribed for 10 days; steroids were tapered at the end of the first month.

document_sections.heading: Laser Photocoagulation
document_sections.content: When the retina surrounding the tear was attached, indirect laser photocoagulation was performed around the tear within the following 72 hours. Persistent subretinal fluid preventing laser uptake during the following 5 days defined failure, because the gas bubble was expected to start shrinking after 5 days. For 360-degree laser retinopexy, treatment of flat retina between the ora serrata and equator began before PR. After PR, laser was applied around the tear and the earlier treatment was completed to 360 degrees. Patients were instructed to maintain head positioning for several days after laser treatment to allow chorio-retinal adhesion at treated sites. Examinations occurred on the first day, at the first week, and at the first and second month; subsequent follow-up depended on clinical status. Primary success meant an attached retina at the end of 2 months without further surgery. Failure included a retina that had not flattened sufficiently for laser by the fifth postoperative day, failure to obtain reattachment, or renewed detachment as the bubble shrank. PPV was the preferred treatment after failure. Cryotherapy was not used.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Descriptive analyses addressed demographics, presentation findings, and anatomic and functional outcomes. Analyses used SPSS software (version 23.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Categorical data were expressed as counts and percentages; continuous data as median (interquartile range). Skewed between-group data were compared with the Mann Whitney U test, and categorical between-group data with Chi square or Fisher’s exact tests. Statistical significance was defined as p <0.05.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Records from 24 eyes of 24 patients were reviewed. Three cases were excluded after loss to follow-up, leaving 21 eyes of 21 patients. Median age was 59, with a range of 18 to 68. The cohort comprised 14 (66.7%) men and 7 (33.3%) women; 13 (61.9%) eyes were phakic and 8 (38.1%) pseudophakic. Median detachment extent was 4 (2-7) clock hours. At the assessment reported here, 20 (95.2%) eyes had one break and one (4.8%) patient had 2 breaks; the abstract instead reports one preoperative break in 19 cases. The macula remained attached in 16 (76.2%) eyes and was detached in 5 (23.8%). Laser retinopexy over 360 degrees was performed in 18 (85.7%) patients. PR failed in 8 cases (38.1%); these patients underwent PPV, which identified additional breaks in 4 of them. After a median follow-up of 10 months (4-38), PR was considered successful in 13 (61.9%) eyes that remained attached. One case classified as successful developed another detachment 9 months after PR because of a new break beside earlier laser treatment; this patient received PPV with silicone oil tamponade. No PR-attributable adverse event, including increased IOP or endophthalmitis, was observed. Successful cases developed neither subsequent PVR nor epiretinal membrane (ERM). Comparisons of successful and failed cases appear in Tables 1 and 2. Age, gender, visual acuity, lens status, macular involvement, detachment extent and break count had no significant association with outcome; 360-degree laser retinopexy was significantly associated with anatomic success.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: Despite improvements in vitrectomy, including smaller incisions and higher cut rates, the authors regard PR as an option for selected RRD cases with fewer complications than SB and PPV. Published PR success rates range from 44% to 94%, averaging 74.4%; the authors consider their 61.9% success rate consistent with that literature. A review of 422 cases reported 60.7% success with PR alone, and Cohen and co-workers reported 59.5% primary PR success. Although reported success rates for PPV (71-96.7%) and SB (68.2–93.7%) are somewhat higher, PR is fast, inexpensive, potentially office-based and associated with relatively few complications. The authors contrast it with complications associated with PPV and SB, including iatrogenic retinal breaks, PVR, cataract formation, pain, explant extrusion and ocular motility problems. Reported serious PR complications include infectious endophthalmitis and giant retinal tear; anterior-chamber gas leakage has also been reported. Their series had no adverse effect attributed to PR. Rootman and co-workers identified large tears, pseudophakia and PVR as the three principal factors associated with PR failure; accordingly, the authors stress careful preoperative assessment of break number and location. Significant cataract in phakic eyes, or capsular phimosis or posterior capsular opacification in pseudophakic eyes, can hinder peripheral examination, allow small breaks to be missed and interfere with laser treatment. Other reports suggest lens status is not a significant determinant of PR success. This series likewise found no significant association, although the authors consider its small sample a possible influence on that finding. Laser retinopexy matters because PR does not remove the traction responsible for a tear: the bubble presses detached sensory retina against the retinal pigment epithelium, while laser seals the break after attachment and helps prevent reopening as gas diminishes. The authors propose that 360-degree treatment between equator and ora serrata can also guard against failure from new or overlooked breaks. They avoided PR in grade C or worse PVR because traction and retinal shortening may resist reattachment. New breaks are a major concern: spaces in liquefied vitreous and movement of expanding gas may create shearing forces and additional vitreoretinal traction. A break missed before treatment may also compromise success. The authors view these possibilities as the rationale for 360-degree laser retinopexy, the only significant success factor in their series, although 3 cases developed recurrent detachment despite laser. Earlier studies reported that new breaks occurred predominantly in lower or previously unaffected quadrants. Investigating new breaks responsible for failure was outside this study's scope. Another patient developed retinal detachment 9 months after PR from a new break beside the original one, despite having received 360-degree laser; the authors question whether that event should count as failure. Mudvari et al reported that renewed detachment occurred mostly during the first 4 weeks after PR, while other evidence indicates it can occur during the first year. No successful case developed PVR or ERM, although vitreomacular interface abnormalities, especially ERM, have been described as expected PR complications. Outcomes of PPV after failed PR were outside this study's scope. Evidence on lattice degeneration is conflicting: one report associated involvement larger than 3 clock-hours with failure through extensive vitreoretinal adhesions, whereas other reports found no association with unfavorable outcomes. The authors did not consider lattice degeneration when choosing surgery and identify this as a possible shortcoming. Their principal limitations are retrospective design and small sample size. As a tertiary referral center, their clinic usually sees complex RRD with substantial PVR, potentially biasing treatment selection. They also did not assess detachment duration, which they expect could be linked to worse outcomes when symptoms persist longer. They conclude that PR is a suitable surgical option for selected RRD cases, offering a reasonable favorable-outcome rate with limited discomfort, adverse effects and complications.
